releases.notes:
### Added
- **The mod catalogue grew from 24 profiles to 45 families**, and every one of them is
  dated against upstream. The new families are the ones that change an audit rather
  than decorate it:
  - identity: `floodgate`, `fabricproxy-lite`, `easyauth`;
  - protocol: `viabackwards`, `viafabricplus`;
  - services beside the game port: `bluemap`, `squaremap`, `journeymap_webmap`, `e4mc`,
    `plasmovoice`;
  - code execution: `carpet` (Scarpet), `computercraft` (HTTP API), `minescript`;
  - client inspection: `trustedclients`;
  - permissions and claims: `openpartiesandclaims`, `fabric-permissions-api-v0`, `worldedit`;
  - logging: `ledger`, `fastback`;
  - what the client tells other people: `nochatreports`, `essential-container`,
    `customskinloader-bootstrap`, `no-telemetry`, plus `chunky`.
- **`ModVerification`**: one dated upstream check per family -- the project page, the
  version the loader reports, whether a build exists for 26.3, and the date. The report
  prints the date, and says so once the table is more than six months old.
- **`ModCatalog.Focus`**: the question an audit asks about a mod, separate from where it
  runs. Identity, code execution and client inspection are raised to MEDIUM because they
  change the meaning of every other finding; the rest are summarised as questions.
- 24 tests and 3 self-test checks: id coverage, alias resolution, dated checks, the
  staleness rule with an injected date, and a guard that `docs/mod-catalogue.md` lists
  every family.

### Changed
- **Three ids in the catalogue could never have matched an installed mod.** The loader
  reports `roughlyenoughitems` (not `rei`), `xaerominimap` (not `xaeros-minimap`) and
  `voicechat` (not `simple-voice-chat`). Every id is now read out of the published jar's
  `fabric.mod.json`; the old names stay as aliases so nothing that used to resolve stops
  resolving.
- **A published `-SNAPSHOT` release is no longer called a working-tree build.** Geyser,
  ViaVersion and ViaBackwards ship releases named that way. A version string equal to the
  one the catalogue saw upstream is a release; anything with git metadata still is not.
- Version drift is reported, not judged: an installed version that differs from the
  catalogue check is listed with both strings and the date, and never described as
  outdated.
- The WorldEdit entry in `CatalogApplicability` now records 7.4.6 as the newest release
  seen (it was 7.4.5), verified on Modrinth today.

releases.notes:
### Added
- **Every catalogued plugin now carries a version verdict.** `CatalogApplicability`
  answers, for each of the 18 entries, what it applies to, which version fixed it,
  the newest upstream release seen, the date of the check and what the check rests
  on. The table is printed by `show exploits`, attached to each finding from
  `auxiliary/audit/plugin_exploit_surface`, and prepended to every artifact
  `auxiliary/payloads/poc_artifact` writes, so a file read months later still says
  which builds it describes.
- 15 tests and 4 self-test checks. `CatalogApplicabilityTest` asserts the verdict
  table covers exactly the catalogue, that every verdict is dated, and that a fixed
  or obsolete entry names the version that ended it. `PocArtifactApplicabilityTest`
  writes real files into a temporary audit folder and reads them back: the header
  is there, the catalogued body is unchanged, revert removes the file, and no entry
  that is fixed upstream can still write an artifact at all.

### Changed
- **Geyser's player-head URL fetch is marked FIXED, not open.** It affects
  `<= 2.9.2` and is patched in `2.9.3` (CVE-2026-42188 / GHSA-xcfg-fcr5-gw9r).
  The entry stays in the catalogue as knowledge; a server at or above 2.9.3 will
  not reproduce it, and the finding says so instead of implying a live bug.
- **WorldEdit's schematic entry is marked OBSOLETE** (`< 7.4.4`, fixed `7.4.4`,
  7.4.5 current). It has no artifact and is kept so the name is recognised rather
  than silently dropped.
- MythicMobs stays `UNVERIFIED` with the newest release seen (5.13.0): no advisory
  was confirmed for the deserialisation path, and the entry says "not confirmed"
  rather than borrowing the confidence of the checked ones.
- `docs/threat-model.md` now states the actual boundary for drop-in Java modules:
  they are unrestricted user code inside the game process, and the gate governs
  the modules this build ships, not code you drop in.

releases.notes:
# 0.2.0-beta.16 — the mods, not just the plugins

Until now the tool audited plugin surfaces. This release audits mods: what is
loaded, what it does to an audit, and — for the first time — something about the
other end.

## `auxiliary/audit/mod_posture`

Reads the mod loader's inventory and sorts it by what it means:

| What it is | Examples | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Changes what the server accepts | Cobblemon, LuckPerms, Create, Lithium, ViaVersion | Every finding about permissions or versions has to be read through these |
| Opens a service beside the game port | Simple Voice Chat, Geyser, spark viewer, LuckPerms web editor | A network question the game's permission system cannot answer |
| Client only | Sodium, Iris, JEI, REI, EMI, Distant Horizons, maps | A visual difference found with these installed is not a server finding |
| Library | Fabric API, Cloth Config, Architectury | A version conflict here breaks its dependants |
| World generation | Terralith | Changes terrain, not permissions |

It also flags two things that quietly invalidate everything else: two jars of the
same mod, and build strings that came from a working tree rather than a release.

## The first real evidence about the far end

A custom payload's **identifier** names the channel a mod registered. `cobblemon:main`
on the wire means Cobblemon is registered on the other side. `PacketTelemetry` now
keeps those identifiers — bounded to 64, never a payload body, never written to the
audit log.

It is genuinely the closest a client gets to a server mod list, and it has a hard
limit that the module states in its own output: the identifier is only nameable when
this client has the mod that decodes it. On a vanilla client the same server traffic
is undecodable and invisible.

## What this does not do

It does not list the server's mods, and it says so in a finding rather than a
footnote. It does not claim any mod is vulnerable: the catalogue describes what each
family does that is worth reviewing, and carries no CVE numbers I cannot verify.

## Numbers

- 281 JUnit tests, 0 failures (10 new in `ModPostureTest`).
- 139 `--self-test` checks (2 new).
- `ModCatalog`: 24 mod families. `ModPosture` is pure and lives in core, so the
  report is testable without a game.

## On the licence text

Cobblemon is **MPL-2.0** (Cable-MC, `gitlab.com/cable-mc/cobblemon`). Nothing in
this release copies, links against or redistributes Cobblemon code, so this work
does not depend on any agreement with Cable-MC. Champions Code remains IDI's own
project under IDI's All Rights Reserved licence.

## Still not verified

- Windows and a real Minecraft 26.3 client: not run here. `FabricLoader.getAllMods()`
  and the channel capture compile against the 26.3 mappings and are covered by unit
  tests on the analysis, not by launching the game.

releases.notes:
# 0.2.0-beta.15 — discovery tier, and eight more plugin families

Four new modules. All of them work from the command tree the server already sent
this account, and none of them sends anything.

## New

| Module | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `auxiliary/scanner/plugin_fingerprint` | Names the plugin families the advertised roots point at, lists which of them the exploit catalogue has entries for, and hashes the sorted roots so two scans of one server compare equal and a changed surface does not. |
| `auxiliary/audit/admin_command_exposure` | Classifies the tree into authority, code, moderation, world, player and disclosure capabilities and reports which this account was offered. |
| `auxiliary/audit/alias_shadowing` | Bare names claimed by more than one provider, vanilla names a plugin now answers, duplicate subcommand literals. |
| `auxiliary/audit/client_trust_posture` | Offline mode, platform brand, protocol self-description and resource-pack policy, each with what it does and does not establish. |

`PluginRiskReviewModule` went from 16 to 24 families: LuckPerms, PlaceholderAPI,
Plan, Dynmap, LiteBans, Simple Voice Chat, AuthMe and CMI. Its profile table is now
shared with the fingerprint module, so both name a family the same way.

## Why the fingerprint matters

```
fingerprint a3f10c8de2b41e77
```

That string is SHA-256 over the sorted bare roots the server advertised, truncated
to 16 hex characters. Scan before a plugin update and after it: equal means the
surface did not move, different means something was added, removed or renamed.
"Has the server changed since the last audit" stops being a memory test.

It is a hash of what this account was offered, not of what is installed: the tree
is permission-filtered per account, so two accounts on one server fingerprint
differently. That is a fact about the tool, stated here so it cannot be mistaken
for a fact about the server.

## Absence is not evidence

Every module here reports a clean result as "nothing matched", never "nothing is
installed". `admin_command_exposure` says a plugin that registers its commands late,
or hides them by permission, sends nothing to classify; `plugin_fingerprint` says a
vanilla server and a heavily filtered tree look the same; `alias_shadowing` says
collisions can exist for names this account was never offered. Those sentences are
in the findings, not in a footnote.

## Numbers

- 271 JUnit tests, 0 failures (17 new in `DiscoveryModulesTest`).
- 137 `--self-test` checks (1 new, which proves the four modules are inside the jar).
- 25 built-in modules, 24 plugin families in the review table, 18 catalogue entries.

## Still not verified

- Windows: `.\gradlew.bat`, `desktopSelfTest` and `--demo` have not been run here.
- Minecraft 26.3: the mod has not been launched in a client this session. The new
  modules are covered by unit tests against fixed command trees, not by connecting
  to a real server.

releases.notes:
# 0.2.0-beta.14 — plug-and-play payload modules

The question this release answers: are the payloads rerouted towards the
plug-and-play system? The enforcement was; two things were not.

## What was already true

The payload rules are enforced **by interface, not by class identity**.
`ChampionConsole.runActive()` asks `module instanceof PayloadModule` and, for
anything that answers yes:

- calls `effect(options)` before the authorization gate and refuses the run if
  `PayloadSafety` rejects it,
- prints the declared effect and the revert plan,
- names the effect in the payload banner and in the audit line.

A module compiled from a dropped-in source file goes through the same code. The
collection repository already ships one payload module this way:
`auxiliary/payloads/seed_disclosure`, which declares `chatCommand("/seed")`.

## What was not

**1. The audit folder was only handed out at construction.** `ChampionConsole`
injected `AuditFolder` into the modules it was built with. `registerModule(...)`
and `replaceExternalModules(...)` — the paths every drop-in, runtime-compiled and
example module arrives through — did not. A payload module that declares an
artifact therefore had nowhere to write and reported *"this front end has no
artifact folder"*. Both paths now inject it.

**2. The template taught the wrong contract.** `ExamplePayloadModule`, the file
`docs/exploit-and-payload-files.md` tells you to copy into the payload folder,
implemented only `ResearchModule`. A module built from it declared no effect,
skipped the `PayloadSafety` check, and showed no payload banner — the opposite of
what that folder is for. It now implements `PayloadModule` and
`ArtifactFolderAware`, declares `example_plan.txt`, writes it into the audit
folder, and sends nothing.

## Where each payload lives now

| Module | Path | Declared effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `auxiliary/payloads/poc_artifact` | built in | `auditArtifact(entry file)` from the catalogue |
| `auxiliary/payloads/fixture_reproduction` | built in | `auditArtifact(plan)` for `ACTION=PLAN`, none for `VERIFY` |
| `auxiliary/payloads/chat_reach_proof` | built in | `chatCommand("/say champions-proof <tag>")` |
| `auxiliary/payloads/example_plan` | plug-and-play example | `auditArtifact("example_plan.txt")` |
| `auxiliary/payloads/seed_disclosure` | collection repository | `chatCommand("/seed")` |

Both routes reach the same gate, the same safety check and the same audit log.

## Numbers

- 254 JUnit tests, 0 failures (3 new: folder injection on both dynamic
  registration paths, and refusal of an unsafe declared effect before the module
  body runs).
- 136 `--self-test` checks.
- 18 catalogue entries, 10 mechanisms, 9 payloads, 21 built-in modules,
  7 in the collection repository.

## Still not verified

- Windows: `.\gradlew.bat`, `desktopSelfTest` and `--demo` have not been run here.
- Minecraft 26.3: the mod has not been launched in a client this session. The
  registration change is covered by console tests, not by dropping a real file
  into the module folder and watching it register.
